summary:
GAIA is a pipeline and interactive web map that uses NASA-ISRO NISAR radar satellite data to measure ground deformation along the East African Rift, from Afar to Mozambique. The rift is slowly splitting the African plate. It produces earthquakes, magma intrusions and landslides, often in areas with little ground monitoring.

When a USGS earthquake occurs, GAIA automatically builds a search area and time window around the epicenter. It finds matching NISAR interferograms through the Alaska Satellite Facility and streams only the HDF5 datasets it needs. This is about 6% of each roughly 1 GB file, so no full download is required. It converts radar phase into centimeters of line-of-sight ground motion, masks low-quality pixels, and stitches frames into regional mosaics. Ascending and descending passes are combined to separate vertical uplift or subsidence from east-west plate opening.

The dashboard overlays these results on live earthquakes, active fault traces, plate boundaries and critical infrastructure, and adds a hazard score for decision support. Case studies include the Hayli Gubbi eruption and the Gofa landslide.

This matters because radar sees through cloud and at night. GAIA turns petabyte-scale satellite data into fast, actionable hazard information for regions that lack dense ground instruments.
details: GAIA turns NISAR radar data into a ground-motion map of the East African Rift. A user can enter an area and dates, or let GAIA react automatically to a USGS earthquake. In the automatic case it builds a bounding box (about ±1°) and a time window (about ±12 days) around the epicenter. It then queries the Alaska Satellite Facility for NISAR geocoded unwrapped interferograms. Instead of downloading about 1 GB per granule, it uses HTTP range requests to stream only the needed HDF5 datasets, about 6% of each file. Phase is converted to line-of-sight displacement in centimeters, low-coherence pixels are masked, and frames are leveled, feather-blended and resampled to Web Mercator into regional mosaics. Ascending and descending passes can be combined to separate vertical motion from east-west plate opening. A Leaflet dashboard shows the results alongside live USGS earthquakes, GEM active faults, plate boundaries and critical infrastructure. A multi-sensor module combines InSAR with rainfall, soil moisture, earthquake swarms and SO₂ into a 0–100 risk score. An inverse-velocity module estimates time to failure.
